text: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch, also known as the Pacific trash vortex or North Pacific Garbage Patch, is a gyre of marine debris located in the central North Pacific Ocean, roughly between 135°W and 155°W, and 35°N to 42°N. It receives plastic and floating trash from the Pacific Rim, including countries in Asia, North America, and South America. Despite popular belief, the patch does not appear as a visible island of garbage; instead, it consists of a widely dispersed area with a low density of 4 particles per cubic metre (3.1/yd³), making it undetectable by satellite imagery or casual boaters and divers. The debris is primarily composed of suspended microplastics—particles as small as fingernail-sized or smaller—that float in the upper water column. Researchers from the Ocean Cleanup project estimated the patch covers 1.6 million square kilometres (620,000 square miles), equivalent to about twice the size of Texas, and contains 45,000 to 129,000 metric tons (50,000 to 142,000 short tons) of plastic as of 2018. By the end of 2024, Ocean Cleanup had removed over one million pounds of trash, representing 0.5% of the total accumulated waste. While microplastics dominate by count, 92% of the mass comes from larger objects, including plastic lighters, toothbrushes, water bottles, pens, baby bottles, cell phones, plastic bags, and nurdles, some of which are over 50 years old. The patch is rapidly accumulating, increasing by 10-fold each decade since 1945, and contains approximately six pounds of plastic for every pound of plankton. A similar patch exists in the Atlantic Ocean, known as the North Atlantic garbage patch. The patch was first predicted in a 1988 NOAA paper based on research by Alaska-based scientists who observed high concentrations of marine debris in the North Pacific, particularly in regions influenced by ocean currents, leading to the hypothesis of a stable accumulation zone in the North Pacific Gyre. Charles J. Moore, after returning from the Transpacific Yacht Race in 1997, reported encountering a vast stretch of floating debris and alerted oceanographer Curtis Ebbesmeyer, who named the area the "Eastern Garbage Patch" (EGP). The JUNK Raft Project, a 2008 trans-Pacific voyage organized by the Algalita Marine Research Foundation, aimed to highlight the plastic pollution in the patch. In 2009, Project Kaisei/Ocean Voyages Institute vessels, the New Horizon and the Kaisei, conducted a research voyage to assess the feasibility of large-scale collection and recycling, supported in part by the Scripps Institute of Oceanography's 2009 SEAPLEX expedition, which also studied the impact of plastic on mesopelagic fish like lanternfish. In 2010, Ocean Voyages Institute conducted a 30-day expedition in the gyre to continue scientific research and test prototype cleanup devices. In July/August 2012, the institute sailed from San Francisco to the eastern limits of the North Pacific Gyre, ending in Richmond, British Columbia, and returned, focusing on tsunami debris from the 2011 Japanese earthquake. A 2015 study found that debris from Asia primarily originates from six countries: China, Indonesia, the Philippines, Vietnam, Sri Lanka, and Thailand, with China responsible for about 30% of plastic ocean pollution as of 2010. In 2017, the Ocean Conservancy reported that China, Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand, and Vietnam collectively dump more plastic in the sea than all other countries combined. Efforts to reduce land-based debris have been led by organizations such as the Coastal Conservancy, Earth Day, Ocean Cleanup, and World Cleanup Day. A 2019 study estimated that 80% of ocean plastic comes from land-based sources, with 20% from boats and marine activities; a 2018 study found that synthetic fishing nets accounted for nearly half the mass of the patch due to ocean currents and increased fishing activity. A 2022 study indicated that 75% to 86% of plastic pollution stems from fishing and agriculture, with emissions primarily from Japan, China, South Korea, the U.S., and Taiwan. A 2020 study identified the U.S. as the third-largest contributor of plastic pollution in coastal environments. After China banned plastic imports in 2018, countries with poor waste management, such as Indonesia, became dumping grounds for U.S.-origin plastic. A 2019 study of 6,093 debris items over 5 cm found that 99% of rigid items by count and 90% of the total debris mass (514 kg) were plastics, traced to five industrialized fishing nations. The hard plastic waste includes unidentifiable fragments, fishing and aquaculture gear (nets, fish boxes, oyster spacers, eel traps), and household items. Of 201 analyzed objects, the most common languages were Chinese, Japanese, English, and Korean. The Ocean Cleanup estimated that up to 86% of the plastics in the patch come from fishing activity. The patch formed gradually through ocean currents capturing waste from coastal waters off North America and Japan, which are drawn toward the center by the gyre's rotational pattern. A 2014 study found that discarded fishing gear, such as buoys, lines, and nets, accounted for over 60% of the mass of marine plastic debris. According to a 2011 EPA report, the primary source of marine debris is improper waste disposal, including littering and illegal dumping, occurring at land-based sites like marinas, ports, rivers, harbors, and storm drains, as well as at sea from fishing vessels and cargo ships. Debris ranges from miles-long abandoned nets to micro-pellets used in cosmetics and cleaners. A computer model predicts that debris from the U.S. west coast would travel to Asia and return to the U.S. in six years, while debris from the east coast of Asia would reach the U.S. in one year or less. Although microplastics make up 94% of the estimated 1.8 trillion plastic pieces, they account for only 8% of the 79,000 metric tons (87,000 short tons) of plastic, with the majority from fishing. A 2017 study concluded that of the 9.1 billion metric tons of plastic produced since 1950, nearly 7 billion metric tons are no longer in use, with 9% recycled, 12% incinerated, and 5.5 billion metric tons (6.1 billion short tons) in oceans and land. A 2021 study found more than 40 animal species on 90% of the debris studied, and a 2022 study suggested that the patch supports a thriving ecosystem of life, including coastal species like jellyfish and sponges, which survive and reproduce in the open ocean. Scientists are concerned that this mix may create unnatural "neopelagic communities" where coastal species compete with or consume open-ocean species. The patch's size is indefinite and its debris distribution is not precisely defined due to the rarity of large items; most debris consists of small particles that evade detection. The estimated size of 1.6 million square kilometres (about twice the size of Texas or three times the size of France) is based on sampling, though such estimates are conjectural due to sampling complexities and the lack of a standard to define "elevated" pollution levels. Net-based surveys, using neuston or manta trawl nets with 0.33 mm mesh, are less subjective than direct observations but are limited by net size and ship time, requiring many tows to capture average abundance. Long-term data show a dramatic increase in plastic abundance in the North Pacific Subtropical Gyre: in 1999, plastic abundance was 335,000 items per square kilometre (870,000/sq mi) and 5.1 kilograms per square kilometre (29 lb/sq mi), roughly ten times higher than in the 1980s, with similar increases off Japan. However, extreme spatial heterogeneity and the need to compare equivalent water masses mean such findings must be interpreted with caution. In August 2009, the Scripps Institution of Oceanography/Project Kaisei SEAPLEX survey found plastic in 100 consecutive samples across 1,700 miles, showing that the patch contains larger items but is mostly composed of smaller, "confetti-like" pieces that increase in concentration toward the center, suggesting the affected area may be smaller than estimated. Data from Pacific albatross populations also indicated two distinct debris zones. In March 2018, the Ocean Cleanup published findings from the Mega- (2015) and Aerial Expedition (2016), which used 30 vessels and 652 survey nets to collect 1.2 million pieces, and a C-130 aircraft with LiDAR sensors. The study found the patch covers 1.6 million square kilometres with a concentration of 10–100 kilograms per square kilometre (57–571 lb/sq mi), containing an estimated 80,000 metric tons (88,000 short tons) of plastic, with 1.8 trillion pieces and 92% of the mass in objects larger than 0.5 centimetres (3/16 in). NOAA clarified that the term "Great Pacific Garbage Patch" misrepresents the situation, as the area is not a large, visible mass of debris and cannot be seen from space. A 2001 study found plastic concentrations at 334,721 pieces per square kilometre (866,920/sq mi) with a mean mass of 5.1 kilograms per square kilometre (29 lb/sq mi), seven times greater than zooplankton in many areas, and much lower concentrations in deeper water. In 2012, researchers Goldstein, Rosenberg, and Cheng found microplastic concentrations had increased by two orders of magnitude over the previous four decades. On 11 April 2013, artist Maria Cristina Finucci founded The Garbage Patch State at UNESCO in Paris. In March 2018, New Scientist predicted the patch's size as approximately 1.6 million square kilometres. In 2010, an IEEE conference argued that the patch poses a threat to human living conditions but is controllable, while a 2011 conference noted it disrupts marine ecosystems and creates new biological conditions, leading to a new ecosystem. In 2009, Ocean Voyages Institute removed over 5 short tons (4.5 t) of plastic during the initial Project Kaisei cleanup. In 2019, during a 25-day expedition, they removed over 40 metric tons (44 short tons). In 2020, over two expeditions, they removed 170 short tons (150 t; 340,000 lb), with the first removing 103 short tons (93 t; 206,000 lb) and the second 67 short tons (61 t). In 2022, over two summer expeditions, they removed 148 short tons (134 t; 296,000 lb) of ghostnets, consumer items, and mixed plastic debris. On 9 September 2018, the first collection system, Ocean Cleanup System 001, was deployed from San Francisco to a trial site 240 nautical miles (440 km; 280 mi) away.

The Ocean Voyages Institute set a record for the largest cleanup by removing 170 short tons (150 t; 340,000 lb) of plastic from the ocean. The first 45-day expedition removed 103 short tons (93 t; 206,000 lb) of plastic, and the second expedition removed 67 short tons (61 t) of plastic from the garbage patch. In 2022, over the course of two summer expeditions, the institute removed 148 short tons (134 t; 296,000 lb) of plastic ghostnets, consumer items, and mixed plastic debris from the garbage patch. On 9 September 2018, the first collection system was deployed to the gyre to begin the collection task. This initial trial run of the Ocean Cleanup Project started towing its "Ocean Cleanup System 001" from San Francisco to a trial site approximately 240 nautical miles (440 km; 280 mi) away. The initial trial of the "Ocean Cleanup System 001" lasted four months and provided the research team with valuable information relevant to the design of the "System 001/B". In 2021, the Ocean Cleanup collected 63,182 pounds (28,659 kg; 31.591 short tons; 28.659 t) of plastic using their "System 002", with the mission running from July 2021 to 14 October 2021. In July 2022, the Ocean Cleanup announced they had removed the first 100,000 kilograms (220,000 lb; 100 t; 110 short tons) of plastic from the Great Pacific Garbage Patch using "System 002" and announced its transition to "System 03", which is claimed to be 10 times as effective as its predecessor. In April 2024, they celebrated a milestone of 10 million kg of trash extracted, and just seven months later in November 2024, they reached 20 million kg of trash removed. The 2012 Algalita/5 Gyres Asia Pacific Expedition began in the Marshall Islands on 1 May, investigated the patch, and collected samples for the 5 Gyres Institute, Algalita Marine Research Foundation, and several other institutions, including NOAA, Scripps, IPRC, and Woods Hole Oceanographic Institute. In 2012, the Sea Education Association conducted research expeditions in the gyre, conducting 118 tows and counting nearly 70,000 pieces of plastic. The coordinates 38°N 145°W (38; -145) are associated with the location.
